results.summary: This design implements a configurable ring oscillator with up to 3853 inverter stages. By connecting one of the output pins to the ring_in input or enabling internal loopback, a ring of a specific length is formed, and the output frequency can be measured. External hardware such as an oscilloscope or logic analyzer is required to measure the frequency and delay between different points in the chain. The design is notable for its large number of stages and the ability to select from many tap points.

This is an 8-bit single instruction computer that implements the SUBLEQ instruction, which subtracts and branches if less than or equal to zero. It has 8 input pins for data, 8 output pins for data, and control pins for run, halted, set_pc, load_data, and out_strobe. The design is a hardware implementation of a minimalist computer architecture, likely intended for educational purposes. No specific external hardware or test setup is described in the documentation.

This is a 4-bit toy CPU based on a design from a German textbook, featuring a 4-bit accumulator and 4-bit instructions with 4-bit operands. It uses external memory and requires a testbed to drive the pins, including a microcontroller program to handle the clock, reset, and tristate data bus. The internal 19-bit state can be scanned out for debugging and visualization. The design is intended as an educational tool to transition from digital design to microprocessors.

This is a demo design that generates VGA video and audio output, intended for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition. It requires external VGA and audio PMODs to be plugged into the board for testing. The design can also be simulated on an ECPIX5 FPGA with appropriate PMODs, and the audio portion can run on an ULX3S using its DAC. The documentation is minimal and does not provide detailed technical information about the implementation.

This project is a union of projects done in a class, as indicated by its title and description. It has 8 input pins and 7 output pins, and requires external hardware such as 7-segment displays and LEDs. The documentation is very sparse, providing only pin names and a list of external hardware, with no explanation of functionality or how to test it. Therefore, it is difficult to determine what the design actually does beyond being an educational exercise.

This design is a binary counter built from D flip-flops, with additional logic gate examples on the bidirectional pins. It is intended to be tested by connecting a 1 Hz oscillator to the clock pin and observing the 8-bit output on LEDs, which count from 0 to 15 and roll over. External hardware includes a 555 timer for the oscillator, switches for input, and LEDs with resistors for output. The project is a first-time Tiny Tapeout submission and serves as an educational demonstration.

This project is a simple single gate design created for workshop validation. It has two input pins and one output pin, and requires external hardware such as an LED display and input switches for testing. The documentation is extremely minimal, consisting only of a one-line description and a note to look at the Wokwi project. It appears to be a basic test or template design with little original functionality.

This is an 8-bit CPU trainer that executes opcodes fed via input pins, with an 8-bit accumulator and four 8-bit working registers. It supports arithmetic and logical operations, shifts, and provides carry and zero flags. The design is tested by providing a 10 kHz clock, loading opcodes and immediate data, and observing results on a 7-segment display or via output pins. It is intended as an educational tool for learning CPU operation.

This design consists of a string of inverters intended to function as a delay line or ring oscillator, with an XOR gate on the bidirectional pins that could be used as a mixer. The outputs are derived from the inputs according to a specific logic function: OUT1 = IN3 ? (IN0 & IN1) : IN2, and OUT0 and OUT2 are the inverse of OUT1. Testing requires basic DC logic signals on the input pins, and no specific external hardware is needed beyond switches or digital inputs. The documentation is brief and the design appears to be an experiment.

This project counts the number of input switches that are turned on, providing the count on its output pins. It is tested by simply flipping the switches and observing the output. No external hardware is required. The design is a straightforward combinational or sequential circuit, likely created as a learning exercise in Wokwi.
